blocks.text: Ruth 1 opens a narrative arc that progresses from famine, death, and Naomi's emptiness toward restoration and communal blessing. The chapter establishes the condition of loss—famine in the land, Elimelech's death, the deaths of both sons—that creates the desperate need addressed throughout the remainder of the book. Naomi's devastation sets the trajectory that will move toward harvest, kinship redemption, and renewal.

Ruth enters the narrative as a Moabite woman belonging to an ancient social world structured by kinship obligations, household economy, and interwoven family responsibilities. Her marriage to Mahlon bound her to Naomi's family, creating relational ties that transcend national identity. This social context—where family loyalty, inheritance rights, and mutual obligation are fundamental—provides the framework for understanding the redemption plot that unfolds in the chapters ahead.

sections.title: Hesed: Covenant Loyalty and God's Character

blocks.text: When Naomi blesses her daughters-in-law, wishing that Jehovah deal kindly with them, she invokes hesed—a term rooted in ancient covenant and kinship language. Rather than describing fleeting emotion, hesed denotes enduring relational commitment and faithfulness. By framing Naomi's language within this ancient Near Eastern understanding of loyalty and obligation, the chapter establishes the relational world in which God's character and human obligation intertwine.
